These conclusions should then become the standard by which religious doctrines were understood and religious texts interpreted.
The texts had to be brought into agreement with reason.
Seen in this light, the progressive side of Muʿtazilite thought becomes much clearer.
The Salafis, by contrast, went so far in denying the role of reason that some of them accepted the literal meaning of Qurʾānic verses that appear to give God bodily features.
These include references to God’s “face,” “hand” and “throne,” examples we discussed earlier.
According to al-Shahrastānī, the Salafis divided into two groups over such verses.
Some interpreted them, but only in ways that the wording itself could naturally support.
This second group simply accepted the verses as Qurʾān revealed by God and saw no need to go any further.
Al-Shahrastānī describes their position in their own words:
“Reason has shown us that God is unlike anything else. He does not resemble any created thing, and no created thing resembles Him. Of this we are certain.
“But we do not know the meaning of expressions such as ‘The Merciful established Himself on the Throne,’ or ‘I created with My two hands,’ or ‘Your Lord came,’ and similar statements.
“We have not been commanded to interpret these verses. What we have been commanded to believe is that God has no partner and that nothing is like Him. Of that we are certain.”
One phrase in this passage deserves attention:
Does this mean that the Salafis accepted reason as one of the sources of religious knowledge?
In fact, they did—but only within very narrow limits.
They accepted a kind of basic reasoning that, in their view, establishes the necessity of God’s existence and His absolute unity, without partner or equal.
From this basic knowledge followed belief in prophecy and in the world to come.
One of the best-known supporters of this refusal to go beyond the text was Mālik ibn Anas (96–179 AH / 714–795 CE), founder of the Mālikī school, one of the four major Sunni schools of law.
In Mālik’s case, this position appears even more conservative and more strictly traditionalist.
He was responding to interpreters who refused to take literally Qurʾānic verses that seem to describe God in bodily terms.
“The Merciful established Himself on the Throne.” (Sūrat Ṭā Hā, verse 5)
Taken literally, this suggests that God has a throne and sits or establishes Himself upon it. The throne is material, and sitting upon it would be a physical act.
“The establishing is known. How it happens is unknown. Belief in it is required. Asking about it is an innovation.”
Mālik therefore forbids even asking how God is established on the throne.
He treats the question itself as a religious innovation.
And in Islam, bidʿa, religious innovation, was associated with error and deviation.
If even the question was condemned, rational interpretation was more objectionable still.
B — The Hanbali current: This current takes its name from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, founder of another of the four major Sunni schools of law, who died in 241 AH / 855 CE.
This was also a Salafi current, but one that accepted a limited form of interpretation.
It corresponds to the first of the two Salafi groups mentioned by al-Shahrastānī: those who interpreted religious texts only in ways that the wording itself could reasonably bear.
Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal became personally involved in the great conflict over the created Qurʾān.
During the final months of the caliph al-Maʾmūn’s life and throughout the reign of al-Muʿtaṣim, he was subjected to a severe religious examination over his position.
At that time, the ʿAbbāsid state had adopted the Muʿtazilite position.
It began testing judges, jurists, religious leaders and officials to see whether they accepted the doctrine of the created Qurʾān.
Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal stood firmly and courageously by the opposite view despite imprisonment and torture.
Many other opponents of the doctrine gave way under pressure, but he did not.
When he finally left prison, he was even more determined in his position.
Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held that the Qurʾān was not created.
He explained his position at length in a work entitled Refutation of the Heretics and Jahmites concerning the Ambiguous Verses of the Qurʾān That They Doubted and Interpreted Incorrectly.
There he responds, for example, to the Jahmites and Muʿtazilites when they cite the verse:
“We made it an Arabic Qurʾān.” (Sūrat al-Zukhruf, verse 3)
They argued that the Arabic verb jaʿala, “to make,” here means “to create,” and that the verse therefore proves that the Qurʾān was created.
Ibn Ḥanbal replies that the word jaʿala is used in the Qurʾān in two different senses.
“Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light.” (Sūrat al-Anʿām, verse 1)
But elsewhere jaʿala means something closer to “to appoint” or “to make into.”
“I am making you an imam for the people.” (Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 124)
Here, Ibn Ḥanbal argues, “making” Abraham an imam obviously does not mean creating Abraham as an imam, because Abraham already existed before he became an imam.
The word must therefore mean an act of appointing or making something into something else.
He applies the same meaning to:
The Qurʾān, he concludes, is therefore an act of God, not something created in the sense intended by the Muʿtazilites.
Ibn Ḥanbal also answers a Jahmite argument based on the verse:
“The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the Messenger of God and His Word.” (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, verse 171)
The Jahmites argued that Jesus was created, and if Jesus is called God’s Word, then God’s Word must also be created.
Ibn Ḥanbal replies that the Qurʾān uses many descriptions of Jesus that are never used of the Qurʾān itself.
Jesus is described as born, as a child, as a boy and as a grown man.
Can those same descriptions be applied to the Qurʾān?
“It is not lawful for us to say of the Qurʾān what we say of Jesus.”
When the Qurʾān calls Jesus “His Word,” Ibn Ḥanbal says, it refers to the creative command:
God said “Be” to Jesus, and Jesus came into existence.
He is not himself the word “Be.”
That word is speech, and the speech itself is not created.

Ibn Ḥanbal then continues by responding both to Christians and to Jahmites over expressions such as “the Word of God” and “the Spirit of God.” The discussion appears on page 30 of the work just mentioned.
We have presented these examples from Ibn Ḥanbal’s arguments so that his method becomes clear.
He limits himself to arguing from the religious texts.
He does not engage with the rational proofs used by the Muʿtazilites.
That is both his position and his method.
Some later Hanbalis went further than Ibn Ḥanbal himself.
They extended the eternity of the Qurʾān beyond its content and argued that the Qurʾān was eternal even in its letters and sounds.
Some went so far as to say:
“Even the leather and the cover are eternal, not only the Qurʾānic codex itself.”
“It is agreed that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, and that what we read, hear and write is the speech of God.
“The words and letters themselves must therefore be the speech of God.
“And since it is agreed that God’s speech is uncreated, these words and letters must themselves be eternal and uncreated.”
“…until the age reached ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kullābī, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī.

“These men belonged to the Salaf, but they took up the discipline of kalām. They defended the beliefs of the Salaf with theological arguments and systematic proofs. Some wrote books, while others taught.”
This statement marks the beginning of a new line within the picture we have just described.
With these thinkers, the Salafi current begins to take on a different form.

It moves beyond the absolute traditionalism of Mālik ibn Anas, beyond the simple refusal to interpret found among some Hanbalis, and beyond Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s limited interpretation based closely on the wording of scripture.
Yet it still remains within the wider Salafi framework.
Al-Shahrastānī is right to place these three thinkers—al-Kullābī, al-Qalānisī and al-Muḥāsibī—inside that framework.
All three belonged firmly to the People of the Sunna and the Community.
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī said of the followers of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb al-Qaṭṭān that:
“They hold most of what we have reported from the People of the Sunna.”
And, as we know, the People of the Sunna rejected the Muʿtazilite teachings on God’s attributes and on the created Qurʾān.
Ibn Kullāb himself, who died in 240 AH / 854 CE, affirmed eternal attributes of God, including speech.
